Senses.Explanation: “Bed-wetting brat” is a cutting personal insult. Dayu seizes Linji and calls him this; Juelang compares clenched hall-sitters to it, Baiyu pairs it with “seeing form and clarifying mind,” Pufu Zhuo rebukes a talkative questioner with it, and Yinyuan places it in a hall-address image. The epithet always addresses or compares a person, but the applications differ and remain separately stated; no retained witness uses it for an actual child or a literal wet bed.

Senses.Explanation: 阿呵呵 is a voiced laugh or exclamation rather than a separate technical term. Gulin Qingmao ends a poem with 阿呵呵 and asks whether listeners understand; Xuefeng Kong joins it to “also strange” in another verse. A single older lamp occurrence by Hengyue Zhen is retained as a secondary transmission, not as the basis of the gloss.

Senses.Explanation: This Chinese transcription names unsurpassed complete awakening in Sanskrit. Zen masters use it when citing scriptures, naming a resolve or a predicted result, and questioning whether awakening is something fixed that anyone can possess or pass on. Yongming Yanshou quotes the Great Nirvana Scripture's promise of complete awakening to those who hear it, then stresses the rare opportunity of encountering the teaching. Chushi Fanqi recalls a demon who vows to seek it only after every being has awakened, then criticizes that posture as a way to keep waiting. Shanduo Zhenzai builds a triple formula: Buddhas raise resolve for this awakening, realize its fruit and speak its teaching. Dahui Zonggao places a prediction of unsurpassed awakening among a sequence of actions shown from a place without fixed dwelling, then says his own speech likewise proceeds there. Dabian Xianquan asks why the Buddha gave predictions of complete awakening if he said he had attained no fixed thing, then turns to the very funeral offering before him. Miyun Yuanwu places the term within a scripture formula on Amitābha's birthday, then playfully claims his own birthday came first. Tianyin Yuanxiu invokes the Diamond Sutra's denial of a fixed attainment while arguing about the transmission verse. Yunwai Xingze compares how people, heavenly beings and hungry ghosts see the same water differently, cites the statement that no fixed thing is named by this term and returns to what is seen here and now.

Ananda is deployed in the Chan record as a named participant in public questions, teaching-seat actions, compilation, and lineage succession. He asks Kashyapa what was transmitted besides the gold-thread robe; Kashyapa calls ‘Ananda,’ Ananda answers, and Kashyapa tells him to knock down the flagpole before the gate. Later masters raise that exchange and question the assembly about it. In a bowl case, Ananda asks the procedure of the seven buddhas, answers the Buddha's name-call, and is told to carry the bowl and go. Elsewhere he strikes the sounding block and asks the World-Honored One to speak, questions the Buddha about an outsider's realization after a silent exchange, is said to compile the sacred words with the opening ‘Thus have I heard,’ and entrusts the eye-treasury of the teaching. These are the Zen record's deployments of Ananda, not a general hagiography.
